That energy input, in a refrigerator, comes from the electricity that runs the compressor motor.Heat, left to its own devices, always flows from a hotter object to a colder object — never spontaneously the reverse. This is one of the most rock-solid statements in all of physics, essentially a restatement of the second law of thermodynamics. A cup of hot coffee left on a countertop will cool down to room temperature; it will never spontaneously get hotter than the room by pulling ambient heat into itself. So the interior of a refrigerator, which needs to be colder than the kitchen surrounding it, is in a thermodynamically "uphill" situation — heat wants to flow from the warm kitchen into the cool box, not the reverse. To keep the inside cold, or to make it colder, the refrigerator has to continuously fight this natural tendency, forcing heat to flow from the colder interior to the warmer exterior.
